title: Network Sniffing
summary: Network sniffing is the passive capture of traffic from a network interface so the adversary can read data in transit. The interface is placed into promiscuous mode so the network card accepts frames not addressed to it, or traffic is copied to a monitoring port and captured there, which enlarges the visible traffic without touching the endpoints. The payoff is reconnaissance and credential theft: protocols that carry authentication material in the clear, such as older file sharing or directory lookups, hand over reusable secrets, and even encrypted sessions leak configuration detail such as service banners, internal addresses, host names, and network segment identifiers that guide later lateral movement. Sniffing also underpins adversary-in-the-middle activity, and in cloud environments traffic mirroring features let an intruder with the right permissions duplicate instance traffic to a capture target. Detection is difficult because capture is passive: defenders look for capture tooling on hosts, interface mode changes, unusual raw socket use, unexpected mirroring sessions in cloud audit logs, and the downstream effects, such as credential reuse from an unexpected source.

beginner.definition: Network sniffing means quietly reading data as it travels across a network. The attacker sets the network card to accept all traffic, not only traffic meant for their machine. It is like listening to a conversation rather than asking questions.
beginner.whyItMatters: Some traffic carries passwords and session details in a form anyone can read. A passive listener is very hard to spot because it sends almost nothing. What is learned can reveal the whole layout of your network. Those details help an attacker decide where to go next.
howItWorks: A normal network card ignores traffic addressed to other machines on the same network segment.
In promiscuous mode the card accepts every frame it can see, and capture software stores them.
On switched networks the attacker needs a mirror port, a span port or a position on the path.
The captured data is filtered and read, looking for logon details, names and service banners.
Broadcast traffic, older unencrypted protocols and misconfigured services give the most away.
In cloud systems, mirroring features can copy virtual machine traffic to a capture target.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where every room has a thin wall. You cannot see your flatmates, but you can hear every phone call through the wall without entering a single room. Nothing is broken and nothing is opened, yet you learn their bank details and their plans. The only defence that truly works is to stop saying secrets out loud.
takeaways: Sniffing is passive collection, so look for capture tools and mirroring rather than attacks.
Encrypt traffic in transit, because unencrypted protocols leak credentials and detail.
Investigate interface mode changes and raw capture activity on your own hosts.

objectives: Explain what promiscuous mode does and how it enables passive traffic capture.
Describe the kinds of information an adversary gains from sniffing, including credentials.
Identify host and network artefacts that suggest capture activity on a segment.
Explain how cloud traffic mirroring can be abused for the same purpose.
Recommend encryption and segmentation choices that limit the value of sniffed traffic.
